topStories.headline: Bruma Is Open: The Ritz-Carlton's Fog-Inspired Cocktail Lounge Arrives on Nob Hill
topStories.dek: The 80-seat lounge opened October 12 inside the hotel's landmark 1909 Neoclassical building, bringing live jazz, afternoon tea, and a liquid-nitrogen martini to 600 Stockton Street.
topStories.body:
A new gathering spot has quietly taken shape atop Nob Hill. Bruma, the signature cocktail lounge and all-day salon at The Ritz-Carlton, San Francisco, opened on October 12 inside the hotel's landmarked 1909 Neoclassical building at 600 Stockton Street. The name is the Spanish word for mist — a direct nod to San Francisco's coastal fog — and the room's design draws from the parlors of Nob Hill's grand historic mansions.

The 80-seat space was designed by Fettle studio and features a hand-etched mirror behind the bar, a custom mural wrapping the perimeter, and the hotel's original fireplace as a centerpiece. The beverage and culinary program was developed in partnership with Lowder-Tascarella Hospitality and runs from lunch through late night, with a showpiece tableside liquid-nitrogen martini service.

The lounge is designed to build a local following beyond hotel guests, with a weekly schedule built around recurring neighborhood programming: Golden Hour Aperitivo on Wednesdays and Thursdays from 4 to 6 p.m., live jazz on Friday evenings, and a Latin fusion band on Saturdays. A Fall Harvest Afternoon Tea, priced at $135 per guest before tax and gratuity, runs weekends through November 22. Hours are Sunday through Thursday 11:30 a.m. to 11 p.m. and Friday and Saturday until midnight.

topStories.headline: A Chronicle Series Asks Who Still Lives in Chinatown — and Where Everyone Else Went
topStories.dek: A two-part San Francisco Chronicle investigation published this week finds that Chinatown's Chinese population has fallen by roughly 26 percent since the late 2000s, as families and working-class residents follow affordable housing to the city's southeast.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's Chinatown has long defined itself as a landing place for Chinese immigrants and their descendants. A new investigative series by the San Francisco Chronicle, with parts published October 13 and October 19, finds that identity increasingly describes where families came from rather than where they live now.

Comparing census estimates from 2006–2010 with 2020–2024 data, the Chronicle found that Chinatown's Chinese population dropped from roughly 12,000 in the late 2000s to around 9,000 in the early 2020s — a decline of about 26 percent — even as the city's overall Chinese share held steady at just above 20 percent. The Richmond and Sunset districts each lost close to 4,000 Chinese residents over the same period. Meanwhile, Bayview-Hunters Point and Portola each gained thousands: Bayview is now about 27 percent Chinese, and Portola is nearly 46 percent.

Demographers and community leaders told the Chronicle the shift is driven by two overlapping forces: working- and middle-class families seeking homes they can afford, and slowing immigration from China — with newer arrivals increasingly Mandarin-speaking rather than Cantonese, and therefore less likely to settle in historically Cantonese Chinatowns.

The series does not frame Chinatown's future as bleak. Major public investments are underway — the $73 million Portsmouth Square renovation broke ground in June and is expected to be complete by mid-2028, and the Chinatown branch library is also in the early stages of a $47.8 million renovation. But the data make clear that the neighborhood's role as the primary port of entry for the city's Chinese community has shifted in ways that three decades of policy and philanthropy have not reversed.

topStories.headline: Jupiter Room Has Missed Summer and Fall Keeps Slipping — Polk Street's Most-Watched Opening Still Has No Date
topStories.dek: Chef Peter Hemsley and bar director Trevin Hutchins have been building out the former Lord Stanley space at 2065 Polk since early 2026; the bar's own website still says 'late 2026,' with windows still papered over.
topStories.body:
For months, Jupiter Room has been the Polk Street opening that feels perpetually imminent. The martini-focused cocktail bar from Michelin-starred chef Peter Hemsley and bar director Trevin Hutchins has been under construction in the former Lord Stanley space at 2065 Polk Street — the corner of Polk and Broadway in Russian Hill — for most of the year. The project was announced for summer 2026, then penciled in for fall. As of early October, the windows were still covered in paper and no confirmed opening date had been set.

The concept is well-defined: gin- and vodka-forward martinis, elevated bar snacks including fries and sliders, late-night hours, and a menu with historical nods to 19th-century San Francisco mixologist Jerry Thomas. The bar's own website now reads simply 'late 2026.' A takeout window facing Broadway has also been reported in planning documents.

Jupiter Room is one of five food-and-drink projects announced along the upper Polk and Russian Hill corridor this fall. Of those, Handroll Hawker opened at 2360 Polk on September 29, and Saru Handroll Bar has been operating nearby for some time. Bageletto, planned for a former Peet's between Broadway and Vallejo, and Lorella bakery at 2139 Polk are also still in buildout with no firm dates. The lounge at the former Lord Stanley — a space that once supported destination-level dining — remains the most anticipated of the group.

moreNews.headline: Broadway Tunnel Still Running One Lane Each Way as Chinatown Health Center Work Continues
moreNews.body: Drivers using the Broadway Tunnel should expect ongoing delays through at least fall 2027. The partial closure — one lane available in each direction during construction — began August 17, 2026, and is tied to seismic retrofitting and other upgrades at the Chinatown Public Health Center, which sits above the tunnel. The closure is one of three simultaneous major construction projects in Chinatown, alongside the $73 million Portsmouth Square renovation (groundbreaking June 9) and the 30-month, $47.8 million Chinatown branch library renovation. SF Public Works is directing motorists to variable message signs at key intersections for alternate routes.
moreNews.sourceName: San Francisco Chronicle / SF Public Works
